newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sergeant pleads innocent to rape charges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sergeant pleads innocent to rape charges.

text.p: Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson pleaded guilty Monday to 11 counts of violating rules against sexual intercourse with female trainees, but said he did not rape any of the women.

He described the sex as consensual and at said that at times it was initiated by the women. Because of that the drill instructor at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground pleaded innocent to charges of raping eight trainees, including five of the 11 with whom he admitted having sex.
In addition, Simpson pleaded guilty to five counts of attempting to establish an improper relationship with trainees by propositioning them.

"She would come to my office and we would engage in conversation ... and one thing would just lead to another, sir," Simpson said in describing for a military judge one sexual relationship with a female trainee.

The description was typical of those he portrayed, in which the tall, well-groomed sergeant and women trainees at Aberdeen's Ordnance Centre and School would strike up an acquaintance that would quickly lead to sex on the sofa of his office or elsewhere during 1995 and 1996.

But in the propositioning cases, Simpson appeared more aggressive: trying to kiss one trainee he blocked with his arms in a doorway, asking another for a date and a hug, and ordering a third to come to his office wearing workout shorts and no underwear.
"Would there be any military purpose in her reporting in PT (physical training) clothes and no underwear?" asked Army Trial Judge Col. Paul Johnston.
"No, sir," replied Simpson.
The Army forbids personal relationships, sexual or otherwise, between drill instructors and trainees.
Simpson, 32, faces a total maximum penalty of 32 years in jail, a dishonourable discharge and forfeiture of pay and allowances for the violations he pleaded guilty to Monday.
He faces an additional 78 counts of sexual misconduct, including 21 counts of rape.
Jury selection, originally scheduled for Monday, is to begin Tuesday, and opening statements in his court martial trial are likely to start Friday, defence attorneys said.

Simpson is the first of 10 soldiers charged in the military's biggest sex scandal since the 1991 Tailhook affair to go to trial, and he has been charged with the most crimes. Four other cases have been resolved through plea agreements or administrative proceedings.
Simpson's attorneys said he made his plea Monday because he was prepared to take responsibility for those violations, while denying charges of rape or other non-consensual sex violations.
"Our position is that Sgt. Simpson is not afraid of the truth," civilian attorney Frank Spinner told reporters after the pleas were accepted by Johnson.
The attorneys said there was no plea agreement, and said they have chosen to allow the jury to be informed of the pleas.
An Army spokesman, speaking on condition of anonymity, said prosecutors disagreed that the Simpson admitted having with the five women was consensual.
"The government's position is these were not consensual. These were in fact rape," he said.
Simpson's attorneys said Monday there was a "breakdown in discipline" at Aberdeen.

"If Sgt. Simpson is going to come in and accept responsibility for his role, then I think it may be time also for the leadership at Aberdeen Proving Ground to also recognise the fact that discipline had broken down in a significant way on this post," Spinner said.
